_comment: TEMPLATE for the per-repo profile. /pitlane-setup fills this in by examining the repo, asking
about anything it must not guess, and writing the result to <target-repo>/.claude/worktree-profile.json.
It is COMMITTED to the target repo so a teammate who installs the plugin gets a working
setup with no calibration run of their own.
NO SECRETS IN HERE, EVER. A database password for a seed step is read from the environment or from
the copied .env — never written into a committed file.
Annotation is by `_comment` keys, NOT by `//` comments. It is tempting to sketch this schema
as jsonc for readability, but a real profile has to be parsed by jq and by python3, and neither
accepts comments. Every `_comment` key is ignored by the validator wherever it appears.
Omit any optional block entirely rather than filling it with nulls. Absence is meaningful: no
`runtime` block means TOUCH NOTHING, which is a valid and deliberately offered outcome.
EVERY PATH FIELD IS CONTAINED, AND THAT IS AN ENFORCED INVARIANT, NOT A CONVENTION.
`deps[].dir`, `deps[].lock`, `deps[].copy` (inside its `dir`), `copy[]`, `artifacts[].dir`, `artifacts[].inputs`, `runtime.env.file`,
`runtime.seed` and `runtime.teardown`
are all relative to the repo root and must resolve INSIDE it. Absolute paths, any `..` component,
and empty or `.` values are rejected by validation before anything acts on them.
This is not defensive tidiness: because the profile is committed, it arrives with any branch anyone
pushes, and consumers act on these fields with `cp -al`, file writes and teardown deletion. A `dir`
of `../../..` would put those operations on the main checkout or the home directory — damage
strictly outside the worktree, which is the one boundary this design has to hold.
_comment_shell: How to enter the project's toolchain. Hooks launch from the host shell, where the project's
PHP/Node/Python is usually not on PATH. Empty string means run on the host as-is.
Detected from flake.nix / shell.nix / .envrc / .devcontainer — see reference/detection.json.
_comment_shellArgs: HONOURED, by wt_build_shell_argv() in hooks/scripts/bootstrap-lib.sh. Set it and the plugin uses
it; omit it and the plugin falls back to matching the `shell` string, which is why the field
How the wrapper in `shell` takes the command it wraps:
"argv"   — the command follows as separate arguments: `nix develop --command composer install`
"string" — the command must be ONE argument: `nix-shell --run "composer install"`
Getting it wrong is not a graceful failure. `nix-shell --run composer install` treats `install`
as a nix file to load, and `nix develop --command "composer install"` looks for a binary literally
It is recorded rather than re-derived because string-matching only works for wrappers already on
the list. A hand-written `shell` — `docker compose run --rm app`, an `sh -c` wrapper, a repo's own
`./dev` script — has no entry to match, so a consumer that infers has to guess exactly where
OPTIONAL. When it is absent the plugin matches the `shell` string instead: a wrapper ending in
`--run` or `-c` is treated as "string", everything else as "argv". That fallback is right for
every wrapper in reference/detection.json, and wrong exactly where this field is needed — so
calibration always writes it, and a hand-written profile with an unusual wrapper should too.
_comment_copy: Extra gitignored files to copy in. MERGED with .worktreeinclude, which stays authoritative
Usually empty, and calibration prefers writing a .worktreeinclude to filling this in:
.worktreeinclude is native behaviour that keeps working if this plugin is uninstalled.
Same .gitignore syntax, and the same gitignored-only rule — a tracked file listed here is skipped.
_comment_deps: One entry per dependency directory the repo needs before it can run. At most one per `dir` — see
detection.json's sameDirPolicy for what happens when two lockfiles claim the same directory.
Note the detection side lists `markers` (plural, because one rule can cover both `bun.lock` and
`bun.lockb`) while a profile entry records the single `lock` that was actually found. Detection
matches on any marker; the profile names the one in this repo.
dir           where the dependencies land, relative to the repo root. null means this ecosystem
has no per-project directory (Go), so there is nothing to copy or hardlink.
lock          the lockfile whose content decides whether a copy is still valid.
strategy      install | hardlink | store | skip
install  — run the install command in the new worktree. Correct for any package
manager with its own global content-addressable store (pnpm, bun, uv,
Yarn Berry): the tree is mostly not real disk and sharing it is unsafe.
hardlink — `cp -al` from the main checkout. Correct where the manager materialises
real bytes per project (composer vendor/, npm/classic-yarn node_modules).
Near-instant, almost no disk. NEVER for a Python venv: its scripts and
editable-install mappings name the main checkout, so a linked venv
installs into and imports from main.
store    — the lockfile-keyed shared store. RESERVED: it is a valid schema value
but calibration never proposes it, and nothing builds it yet.
skip     — the plugin does not touch this directory at all. Correct where the
artefacts are build output backed by an already-shared cache
(Cargo target/ + CARGO_HOME, GOMODCACHE). `install` is still recorded
so a developer can see what would populate it, but bootstrap won't run it.
copy          hardlink only: paths INSIDE `dir` (no glob) that bootstrap makes real copies after
the link, because the package manager rewrites them in place and through a shared
inode that write lands in the main checkout — composer's `composer` (vendor/composer/
autoload_*.php, installed.*), npm's `.package-lock.json`, Yarn 1's `.yarn-integrity`.
Detection's `depCopy` records propose it; `[]` means none. A path the dir lacks is
skipped; one that cannot be copied costs the link, and the dir is installed instead.
Absent on a dir whose detection rule lists paths: bootstrap warns once per session.
It cannot cover a package's own install script writing into its directory
(`npm rebuild`, `yarn --force`, composer scripts): run those only where the dir
was installed, or make it `install` (ADR-022).
install       the command that populates `dir`, run inside `shell`.
verify        EXPECTED on every dep that is not `skip`; calibration writes one from the detection
table's per-ecosystem default, or asks the developer. The engine still accepts a dep
without one (older profiles), but then cannot tell a failed install from a usable
tree. bootstrap believes it over the install's exit code. Runs from the worktree
root in the HOST shell (not `shell` — the wrapper can
cost tens of seconds per call). Must not mutate anything, and must actually READ
the installed tree: `composer validate` only checks composer.json/composer.lock
consistency, so it passes identically on a worktree with no vendor/ at all — a
check that cannot fail in the one case bootstrap needs it to.
lockChecksum  `cksum` output for `lock` AS OF CALIBRATION. Evidence, not configuration — see
_comment_evidence. Deliberately stored per-dep rather than in an evidence map keyed
by filename: the JSON reader addresses fields by dotted path, so a key like
"composer.lock" would be unreachable (measured — it splits on the dot).
_comment_artifacts: OPTIONAL. Generated build output the app needs and a fresh worktree lacks, because it is
gitignored: a front-end bundle, a compiled asset dir. Calibration proposes entries from the
output dirs the repo's build writes (detect.sh reports well-known ones as `artifact` hints).
dir     the output directory, with no trailing slash. MUST be gitignored and hold no tracked
file: the plugin clears and replaces it, so the profile is refused otherwise.
inputs  the tracked paths the build reads, lockfiles included: source dirs, the bundler
config, pnpm-lock.yaml. Letters, digits and . _ - @ + / only. When they are identical at
the main checkout's HEAD and the worktree's (`git diff --quiet <main HEAD> HEAD --
<inputs>`) and the main checkout has a non-empty `dir` it gitignores too, that copy is
taken in the background (a hardlink at session start), once the profile is approved.
Otherwise `build` runs in the background after the dependencies, like an install.
build   the command that writes `dir`, run inside `shell`. A command, so the profile needs
approving before it runs (ADR-020). A failed build is not retried until its inputs
at HEAD or the command change, or on `--finish --retry-failed`.
verify  OPTIONAL, EXPECTED: a cheap check that `dir` is usable, run in the host shell. It
decides over the build's exit code, as for deps. Without one, a build must exit 0
and leave `dir` non-empty.
link    `copy` (the default) or `hardlink`: how the main checkout's copy is taken. Copy,
because bundlers rewrite output files in place (measured: esbuild always; vite when
emptyOutDir is off, as in watch mode), which through a hardlink rewrites the main
checkout's build too. `hardlink` only for output nothing rebuilds in place.
Once built or taken, a worktree's build output is its own: keeping it current as the branch
moves is the repo's dev tooling's job, so a later commit to an input does not rebuild it.
KNOWN LIMIT: the main checkout's copy is trusted to match its HEAD. A build made from
uncommitted edits, or not redone since a pull, is taken as it is; the plugin cannot tell.
_comment_runtime: OMIT THIS WHOLE BLOCK to leave runtime alone. Nothing in here is ever inferred: nothing
in a repository states that an env var selects a tenant database, and guessing corrupts data that
is shared with colleagues. Calibration proposes candidates as hints and the developer confirms;
"no runtime isolation" is a valid, offered outcome.
slug      HONOURED. A TEMPLATE: it is expanded and then re-run through wt_slugify(), so even
"{name}" — raw branch text — comes out as [a-z0-9_], which is what everything
downstream trusts a slug to be. That makes it safe by construction rather than by
review, so the template ships the identity mapping "{slug}" and you may change it.
Only {slug} and {name} count as proof that the template varies per worktree; one
containing neither is IGNORED with a warning and the worktree's own name is used,
because the mistake this catches — a constant — would give every worktree one port
and one database.
CHANGING IT RE-POINTS A LIVE WORKTREE: the new slug gets a new database and the old
one is left behind, referenced by nothing.
Capped at 40 characters, because a slug names a database and identifiers stop at 63
or 64 — an over-long one keeps a prefix plus a checksum of the whole, so two long
branch names sharing a prefix cannot collapse onto one database.
port      derived as base + (cksum(slug) % span), where cksum is the first field of POSIX
cksum(1). It is NOT zlib CRC-32 and does not agree with it, so a seed or teardown
script that computes crc32 will name a different port than the hook wrote. base and
span must lie within 1024..65535. A port already claimed by a live sibling worktree
is stepped over; one held by a foreign process only warns. The port RECORDED for a
worktree beats re-derivation, so reopening lands where it was. Teardown must never
kill a port it did not allocate.
env       overrides written INTO the worktree. `file` is a path or a LIST of paths:
every file the app loads, in every environment that needs its own state — a
framework that reads `.env.<env>.local` needs one entry per environment. Each file
gets the same managed block, appended after whatever the file already holds (usually
the developer's configuration, copied in by .worktreeinclude), so the file may and
usually should already exist. This relies on the app's dotenv parser honouring the
LAST assignment of a variable; confirm that for the repo's parser. Each path must be
gitignored and use only letters, digits and . _ - @ + /. A developer takes a file over
by deleting the block, and hands it back by putting the block's first line back.
A var whose value must differ per file is keyed `<file>:<VAR>` in `vars`: it applies to
that one listed file, in place of the shared VAR there.
seed      repo-owned escape hatch — see reference/seed-example.sh for the full contract and a
template. Calibration scaffolds a COMMENTED STUB and never invents its contents: a
database-cloning command is the target repo's business, not this plugin's. It runs
once per worktree, is not retried until its CONTENTS or the slug change, and is
REFUSED outright when any env file is developer-managed, when the other worktrees
cannot be enumerated, or when another live worktree already owns this slug.
teardown  repo-owned, same rule.
serve     the command that starts the app on this worktree's port, run inside `shell` by
/pitlane-serve on request — never by a hook. It must contain {port}, unless the
server reads its port from runtime.port.var in the env files; one with neither
warns, because every worktree's server would then try the same port. A repo whose
start command hardcodes its port gets a serve with the flag spelled out here.
OPTIONAL. It is a command, so the profile needs approving like an install.
stop      OPTIONAL. The command that stops a server serve started, for one that daemonizes
(teardown otherwise signals the process /pitlane-serve recorded, and nothing else).
url       OPTIONAL. Where the app answers: a TEMPLATE using only {port} and {slug}, which must
expand to http:// or https://, a host of letters, digits and . _ -, an optional
port, and a path without spaces, quotes, $, ` or #. It is written as WORKTREE_URL
into every env file's block and into the session's environment, and named in the
session-start notice. One that breaks these rules warns and is not written.
Placeholders: {name} the worktree name as given, {slug} the sanitised name, {port} the derived
port, {worktree} the absolute worktree path, {root} the main checkout.
SUBSTITUTION IS NOT QUOTING. {slug} and {port} are constrained by construction; {name}, {worktree}
and {root} are raw text that can come from a colleague's branch name, so a consumer putting one in
command position must quote it itself. The engine refuses to run an install, build, verify, serve or stop
command, or to write an env.vars value, whose {name}, {worktree} or {root} would carry shell syntax.
_comment_runtime_optout: Not a profile field: a file at `.claude/worktree-no-runtime` INSIDE a worktree makes the engine
skip layer 3 for that worktree alone — no port, no env file, no seed — while dependencies are
still installed. Gitignore it; committed, it turns layer 3 off for the whole team.
_comment_agentNote: Lines of guidance for the model working in a worktree of this repo — what a session cannot learn
from the files in front of it, such as which command runs the tests against this worktree's own
database. One string per line. OPTIONAL: omit it, or leave it [], when there is nothing to say.
It is text from the branch put in front of a model, so it is bounded and it is approved. At most
40 lines of at most 400 characters, and nothing that does not print as itself — no newline, tab or
escape, and no bidirectional, zero-width or tag character inside a line; validation rejects the
profile otherwise. A profile carrying a note needs approval even when
it runs no commands: `bootstrap.sh --review` lists every line as `agent note: ...`, and editing
a line changes the fingerprint, so the edit is approved again before it is shown.
agentNote: Run the test suite with `pnpm test`, never against the main checkout's database.
_comment_timeouts: Bounds on the WORK, in seconds.
THE RULE IS bootstrapSeconds + seedSeconds < the hook's own timeout in hooks/hooks.json (600s),
not each one separately. Both run inside the SAME SessionStart hook invocation, and the platform's
timer starts first. Setting each to 600 — which the earlier draft of this template did — means the
hook is killed at 600s before either internal `timeout` guard ever fires, so the warn-and-continue
path the hooks depend on never runs and the user loses the one thing a hook promises they
A value of 0 is rejected, not honoured: to `timeout` it means no timeout at all, which would turn
the one guard against a hanging bootstrap into an unbounded hang on the session-start path.
The values below leave 60s of headroom under 600s. Raise hooks.json's timeout first if a repo
_comment_evidence: WHAT THIS PROFILE WAS DERIVED FROM. Written by calibration, never edited by hand.
READ, by wt_report_drift() in hooks/scripts/bootstrap-lib.sh, on every bootstrap. All three
fields below are compared, not just the checksums in deps[].lockChecksum: a marker set that has
gained an ecosystem, a shellMarker that means installs now run on the wrong toolchain, and a
detectionVersion older than the shipped table each produce their own warning naming the change
It exists so that cheap deterministic shell can notice the profile has drifted from the checkout
in front of it and say so, instead of applying stale advice in silence.
The comparison is a string compare and a checksum, nothing more — no re-detection, no judgement,
no model. That is what keeps it legal inside a hook, and it warns without ever blocking.
detectionVersion  reference/detection.json's version at calibration time. A newer shipped table
means re-calibrating might propose better answers.
markers           the dependency markers found, sorted. A repo that has since gained
pnpm-lock.yaml has an ecosystem this profile knows nothing about.
shellMarker       which file produced `shell` ("flake.nix", "" if none). A repo that has since
gained a flake.nix is now running installs on the wrong toolchain.
Per-lockfile content lives in deps[].lockChecksum, not here — see _comment_deps.
This whole block is OPTIONAL: a profile without it is valid and simply cannot report drift.
